questions.title: Basic Student Field Encapsulation
questions.question: Implement a `Student` class that encapsulates `name` and `age` fields using the `private` access modifier, exposing them safely through public getter and setter methods[cite: 23].
questions.explanation: Encapsulation is a fundamental object-oriented programming principle that binds an object's internal data together with the operations that manipulate it, restricting direct external access to its internal state[cite: 23]. Declaring fields as `private` ensures they cannot be read or modified directly from outside the class boundary[cite: 23]. Instead, callers must interact through public accessor (`getName`, `getAge`) and mutator (`setName`, `setAge`) methods[cite: 23]. This indirection allows the declaring class to maintain complete control over its internal state, facilitating future implementation changes—such as internal data conversions or logging—without altering external code that depends on the class contract[cite: 23].

If member variables were left public, external code could assign nonsensical values—such as a negative age—compromising object integrity[cite: 23]. By placing validation checks inside mutator methods (`if (age > 0)`), the class acts as a gatekeeper that guarantees only valid data updates internal fields[cite: 23]. When invalid data is passed, the setter can log an error, ignore the request, or throw an exception, ensuring the object maintains consistent internal state throughout its lifecycle[cite: 23].

questions.title: Secure In-Memory Token Vault
questions.question: Design an encapsulated in-memory token vault that stores sensitive credentials as byte arrays and scrubs memory upon explicit disposal[cite: 23].
questions.explanation: Storing sensitive credentials as `java.lang.String` instances creates security risks because immutable strings remain in heap memory until garbage collected[cite: 8, 18, 23]. An encapsulated security vault addresses this by storing credentials as private mutable byte arrays (`byte[]`)[cite: 8, 23]. Access to the secret requires passing a validation lambda or consumer[cite: 23]. When the vault is closed or destroyed, `Arrays.fill(secretBytes, (byte) 0)` overwrites the internal byte array with zeros[cite: 8, 23]. This scrubs the credentials from heap memory immediately rather than waiting for garbage collection[cite: 2, 8, 23].

questions.title: Defensive Architecture Auditor
questions.question: Implement an architectural reflection auditor that inspects a domain model class and verifies that no getters leak mutable collection or array references[cite: 23].
questions.explanation: Enterprise test frameworks use reflection to verify encapsulation and prevent reference leaks across domain models[cite: 10, 23]. An architectural auditor scans a class's methods using `Class.getDeclaredMethods()`[cite: 10, 23]. For every getter returning a collection or array type, the auditor verifies that the returned reference is not identical to the class's internal field[cite: 10, 23]. If a getter returns the same reference as the private field, the auditor flags an encapsulation violation[cite: 10, 23]. This automates encapsulation testing across data access models[cite: 23].
hints: Find getter methods starting with "get" using `Class.getDeclaredMethods()`[cite: 4, 10, 23].
Check if the return type is an array or collection interface[cite: 23].
Verify that calling the getter returns a different reference than the internal field (`field.get(obj) != getter.invoke(obj)`)[cite: 10, 23].

questions.title: Thread-Safe Encapsulated Metric Counter
questions.question: Build an encapsulated statistics collector class that safely aggregates metrics across concurrent threads using atomic variables[cite: 23].
questions.explanation: Encapsulation simplifies concurrency by managing thread-safety internally[cite: 23]. The `MetricsCollector` class encapsulates request metrics using `AtomicLong` counters[cite: 23]. If these counters were exposed directly, external code might perform non-atomic updates or reset values concurrently, causing lost updates[cite: 6, 21]. By encapsulating the fields and exposing thread-safe methods (`recordSuccess()`, `recordFailure()`), the class uses atomic Compare-And-Swap (CAS) instructions internally[cite: 6, 23]. Callers record events safely without managing synchronization locks[cite: 6, 23].
